newsitem.title: USA: U.S., EU meat talks resume next week.
newsitem.headline: U.S., EU meat talks resume next week.

text.p: The United States and the European Union are studying new proposals made in recent days to settle a bitter dispute over meat imports and will resume face-to-face negotiations in Washington next week, the senior U.S. negotiator at the talks told Reuters Wednesday.

EU negotiators had been expected to return to Washington Wednesday to resume discussions, but U.S. negotiator Paul Drazek said it was decided Tuesday night that both sides needed more time to study new ideas that were offered last weekend.
"We decided last night that it would serve our purposes better if we had more time to prepare on both sides for the next series of discussions," Drazek said.
Drazek, senior trade adviser to Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman, said the two sides will continue to communicate via telephones and faxes in the interum.
So far, meetings have been scheduled for next Wednesday and Thursday, but Drazek indicated that the talks could go longer if progress is made.
He would not not comment on any of the new proposals that have been discussed since the negotiators met last week.
"I think it would be better if we had a chance to talk to them ... I don't want to complicate our negotiations next week," he said.
Drazek said the biggest problems in the so-called veterinary equivalency talks remain with poultry issues, but he also noted that "there are issues still outstanding in red meat as well."

The United States and the European Union have been trying to settle a years-old dispute over meat import inspection regulations that has recently blown up into a full-fledged trade war and now threatens the bilateral flow of hundreds of millions of dollars worth of commerce.

The dispute has already halted U.S. poultry shipments to Europe worth potentially around $50 million, and could stop some $300 million worth of European meat products being shipped to the United States if a settlement is not reached.

Washington had threatened to remove over 100 European meat and poultry packing plants from its list of approved exporters by April 15, but on Tuesday extended that deadline until April 30 in hopes an agreement could be reached by then.
